_comment: Economic parameters: harvest yields, spoilage, price curves, upkeep rates. Filled in during Phase 1.
_harvestNote: Weather is drawn from named BANDS rather than a narrow bell curve, so years are memorable: a drought is a disaster you talk about, not a 15% dip. Weighted mean is ~1.02, so the long run is near-neutral while any single year can ruin or make a reign. withinBandJitter adds texture inside a band without blurring the bands into each other.
_forecastNote: forecastBands names which bands the Grain tab's pre-commit outlook runs (issue #46). lean/average/good carry weights 21/25/22 = 68% of the distribution, so the stated range is the USUAL one, not the possible one. FOUR bands sit outside it, not two: drought (5) and poor (12) below, bountiful (10) and glut (5) above — so 17% of years fall UNDER the stated floor, and poor is the larger part of that tail, not drought. The UI names the tail probability rather than implying a floor the simulation does not honour. Widening this to drought..glut would span 0.3x-1.85x and forecast nothing useful. Note 'expected' here means the MODAL band (average, 1.0x), not the distribution mean, which is 1.022.
_storageNote: Grain keeps a couple of seasons, not forever: at 18% a year roughly half survives three years, so a reserve is a real but wasting asset. Was 30%, which combined with a thin surplus put the EQUILIBRIUM reserve at only ~1.3 years — below what a drought (0.3x harvest) requires — so realms could not build a survivable buffer however well they were played, and population declined to extinction over two centuries. The capacity ceiling (in years of consumption) is what actually stops hoarding; spoilage only needs to make grain perishable, not worthless.
_upkeepNote: Per-building upkeep now lives in data/buildings.json alongside each building's other specs. This section only holds cross-cutting upkeep that isn't tied to a single building type.
_warfareNote: F4: military strength is derived from existing stats (garrison, guards, population) rather than a new unit system — consistent with the rest of the game being data-driven stats, not a simulated army. Both sides always take SOME casualty (war has a real cost even in victory), and mitigation is impossible to buy down to zero risk, matching every other risk mechanic in this game (events.ts's own rule: mitigation caps risk, never eliminates it). Land transfer is the closest thing to the research doc's 'geography-gated' territorial consequence available without an actual map.
_warfareTuningNote: Measured after the first implementation: war fired ONCE in 1,200 match-years — dead content. Two causes, both design rather than numbers. (1) warStrength is dominated by the population levy and every ruler grows population similarly, so the best available win probability across 1,200 ruler-years had a median of 0.481 and a MAXIMUM of 0.629; a 0.62 declaration threshold sat in the extreme tail. Nearly every ruler also builds a garrison (mean 0.91 held), so the garrison differentiates nobody. (2) More fundamentally, war traded away the binding resource to gain an inert one: population gates every senior rank (see _populationNote and ranks.json _populationNote), while land is already held at roughly twice what the labour force can work (BACKLOG D3). Winning was close to worthless and losing cost the one thing that mattered. populationTransferFraction fixes the incoherence — conquered territory carries the peasants who work it, which is both historically apt and what makes war a genuine alternative ROUTE to the population-gated ranks that BACKLOG D2 identifies as the whole purpose of F4. Casualties were cut alongside it so the total population swing stays proportionate rather than doubling.
_warfareDepthNote: Phase 18C, answering the playtest note that war 'should be influenced by game — build armies, train, better equipment, and there should be a defenders advantage'. Training and equipment are MULTIPLIERS on the base garrison/guards/levy strength rather than flat additions, so the lever stays meaningful at every scale: a late-game realm with three times the levy gets the same proportional return on drilling its troops as an early-game one, and the ratio that decides a war is scale-invariant. Max levels give 1 + 5*0.15 + 5*0.20 = 2.75x. That number is chosen against warAggression's 0.55 declaration floor: two otherwise-equal rulers sit at p=0.348 (defender-favoured), and a fully-invested attacker against an uninvested equal reaches ~0.60 — enough to clear the floor, but only after roughly 15,000 Taler of investment plus 1,500/yr of standing upkeep, which is a whole early-game treasury. Mutual escalation converges back toward the defender, which is the intended shape: an arms race should not make war cheap. defenderAdvantageMultiplier is deliberately distinct from baseDefenceConstant — the constant is a flat floor that matters most when both sides field almost nothing, while this scales with what the defender actually has, so holding home ground is worth something proportional to the army defending it.

warfare._warBrakesNote: Phase 19A: without memory, a defeated neighbour is a better repeat target (weaker garrison/levy). truceYears is an absolute mutual cooldown after any war between a pair. Weariness accumulates on both belligerents, feeds unrest each year, and decays only in peacetime — so chaining wars against rotating targets still hurts.

_successionNote: F5: a ruler's reign occasionally ends and an heir (same seat, same territory/rank/buildings) inherits — only the accumulated `score` resets. No chance of succession before minReignYears, so a new game/heir always gets a fair run before facing it. Chance then rises with reignYears, capped at maxAnnualDeathChance, so an unusually long reign becomes progressively more likely to turn over rather than running indefinitely.
_starterNote: Baseline human/AI starting realm (docs/kaiser-research.md). Difficulty multipliers scale rivals only — never rewrite these literals in src/engine/starter.ts.
_feedingNote: Kaiser dial fractions of stock at feeding time (min/max/custom bounds) and adequacy bands that drive unrest/disease. Custom percentage is clamped to [customMinPercentage, customMaxPercentage].
_consumptionNote: populationGrainRequirement was 0.5 against a per-peasant yield of 12.5 (5 ha at 2.5) — a 25x surplus, which is not an agricultural economy at all. It made grain worthless, stockpiles meaningless, sabotage loot pointless and weather irrelevant. At 9.0 a peasant produces roughly 1.4x what they eat: an ordinary year leaves a real but modest surplus, a lean year eats into the reserve, and a drought is a genuine famine.
_espionageNote: Guards and saboteurs are STANDING forces with annual upkeep, not one-off purchases. That makes a secret service a recurring burden rather than a bought-once advantage, and gives the late game another cost that scales with ambition.
_eventSeverityNote: Ceiling on how far wealth/population exposure may amplify a single event loss — heavy blow, never instant collapse.
_sabotageNote: Sabotage carries off grain AND a modest share of the treasury, per the original (docs/kaiser-research.md: burns buildings and transfers grain/currency to the attacker). A dedicated raid still takes far more coin; sabotage trades some of that for destroying a workshop outright.
_grainMarketNote: The Kaiser buys surplus corn and sells it back dearer. The spread is what makes storing versus selling a real decision rather than an arithmetic one, and it gives the early game an income source before any market or mill exists.
_populationRatesNote: Rates were 2%/1% for a net +1%/yr, which could not recover from the event pressure Phase 6 deliberately created: measured over 200 years, natural increase plus immigration came to +2,779 while plague and revolt took -2,947, so realms shrank to extinction no matter how well they were played. A pre-modern population facing mortality that heavy needs a correspondingly high birth rate — this is how real medieval populations rebuilt after plague years. Deaths rose too, so the gross churn is high and the NET is a modest +2.1%/yr: recovery is possible but slow enough that a bad decade still hurts for a generation.
